items.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: I was exposed through his tutoring also to composition. After school he would gather us together, a few of the most promising students in music and conduct a harmony class.

ctx.x: Yes. That’s the way I remember it. Well I don’t remember what happened in the Army camps. But when we played locally in Quincy it was a segregated audience at that time. I wasn’t aware of any segregation at that time. It just didn’t register with me that that’s what was going on you know. But it was fun. I enjoyed playing the shows. We had the “end men” in blackface. My father was a member of the chorus I guess you’d call it. And he would have a bass solo and sang a number in the program. But I played in the pit…

Morrison, and I was exposed through his tutoring also to composition. After school he would gather us together, a few of the most promising students in music and conduct a harmony class. So he would teach us how to write music, of course teaching the chords and everything that you would eventually need to know to like compose a march — and that was our first project, was to write a march that you would play in the band, the concert band. So after some of his training, I started writing some pieces. And I wrote…
